modules.standfirst: Three particles, two numbers, one table. Short questions, quick marks — and the 2023 commentary's most alarming line: "many students seemed to have absolutely no concept of what was meant by period number."

subsections.html: An atom is a tiny, heavy, positive nucleus (protons + neutrons) wrapped in shells of almost weightless electrons. Two numbers on the periodic table encode everything the exam asks.

subsections.heading: The three particles and the two numbers
subsections.html:
Spec 1.14, 1.15, 1.16 · 2021 Q1 · 2022 Q2 · 2023 Q1

ParticleRelative massChargeWhere
Proton1+1nucleus
Neutron10nucleus
Electron1/1836 (≈0)−1shells around the nucleus

Atomic number = number of protons (that alone — 2022's scheme ignored any mention of electrons). Mass number = protons + neutrons. So for ¹¹₅B: 5 protons, 11 − 5 = 6 neutrons, and — because atoms are neutral — 5 electrons. Every "how many X" question is one of those three moves.

An atom is the smallest particle of an element; a molecule is two or more atoms covalently bonded together. Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same protons) with different numbers of neutrons — same atomic number, different mass number. Because they have identical electron arrangements, isotopes have identical chemistry.

subsections.heading: Relative atomic mass — the weighted average
subsections.html:
Spec 1.16, 1.17 · 2023 Q9a

Ar is the mean mass of the natural mix of isotopes: Ar = Σ(isotope mass × % abundance) ÷ 100. Copper: (63 × 69.5 + 65 × 30.5) ÷ 100 = 63.61 → 63.6 to 3 sf.

Sanity check before moving on: the answer must sit between the isotope masses, closer to the more abundant one. It is why chlorine's Ar is 35.5 without any atom weighing 35.5.

subsections.heading: Electronic configurations — the 2.8.8 counting rule
subsections.html:
Spec 1.19 · 2023 Q1 · 2025 Q6a

Electrons fill shells from the inside: the first holds 2, the second 8, the third 8 (enough for the first 20 elements). Count the electrons (= protons for an atom) and deal them out:

  • Sodium, 11 electrons → 2.8.1
  • Phosphorus, 15 electrons → 2.8.5 (2025's one-marker)
  • Calcium, 20 electrons → 2.8.8.2

subsections.heading: Reading the periodic table: group, period, ion
subsections.html:
Spec 1.18, 1.20 – 1.22 · 2022 Q2b · 2023 Q1 · 2024 Q1

The table lists elements in order of atomic number; the layout is the electron structure:

  • Group (column) = number of outer-shell electrons. 2.8.4 → Group 4 — "because it has 4 electrons in its outer shell" is the reason mark.
  • Period (row) = number of occupied shells. 2.8.3 has three shells → Period 3. This is the one "many had absolutely no concept of": period counts the rows down, group counts across the top.
  • Group 8/0 (noble gases): full outer shells — unreactive. An element with a full outer shell has 0 electrons available to bond (2024's Q1c answer: 0, allow Group 8).

Ion charge from group: atoms react to reach a full outer shell. Metals in Groups 1/2/3 lose their outer electrons → 1+/2+/3+; non-metals in Groups 5/6/7 gain → 3−/2−/1−. Sodium 2.8.1 loses one → Na⁺, configuration 2.8. Write the charge with its size: +1, not "positive".

The two lookups everything follows from

Group = outer electrons. Period = occupied shells. Get those two straight and every configuration, group, period and ion-charge question is arithmetic.

questions.promptHtml: An atom has the electronic configuration 2.8.3. Without being told the element, state its group, its period, the charge on its ion, and — using a periodic table — its identity.
questions.answerHtml:
Group 3 — three outer electrons. Period 3 — three occupied shells. Ion: loses the three outer electrons → 3+ (configuration 2.8).

Identity: 2 + 8 + 3 = 13 electrons = 13 protons → atomic number 13 → aluminium.

Same-numbers-different-meanings is the trap: "3" appears as both group and period here by coincidence. Group counts the outer electrons; period counts the shells. The 2023 cohort mixing them up is why this question keeps returning.

questions.promptHtml: Chlorine has two isotopes, ³⁵Cl (75%) and ³⁷Cl (25%). Explain why the two isotopes react identically, and calculate Ar.
questions.answerHtml:
Identical chemistry: both have 17 protons and therefore 17 electrons in the same arrangement (2.8.7). Chemical behaviour is decided entirely by the electrons — the extra two neutrons in ³⁷Cl change only the mass.

Ar = (35 × 75 + 37 × 25) ÷ 100 = (2625 + 925) ÷ 100 = 35.5.

Check: between 35 and 37, closer to 35 (the abundant one). ✓

questions.promptHtml: Why does an atom of element X with 14 protons, 14 electrons and 15 neutrons have a mass number of 29 — and why are answers of 14, 15 and 28 each wrong in a different way?
questions.answerHtml:
Mass number counts what has mass in the nucleus: protons + neutrons = 14 + 15 = 29.

The wrong answers (this was 2022's actual MCQ, distractors and all): 14 is the proton count — the atomic number, not the mass number. 15 is just the neutrons. 28 is protons + electrons — but electrons weigh ≈1/1836 of a proton, effectively nothing, and never contribute to the mass number.

questions.promptHtml: Sodium's ion is Na⁺ but its configuration is 2.8.1. Talk through what the atom loses, what the ion's configuration becomes, and why the exam refuses the answer "positive" for the charge.
questions.answerHtml:
The single outer electron is lost (it is the easiest route to a full outer shell). The ion's configuration is 2.8 — eleven protons now hold ten electrons, so the net charge is +1.

"Positive" was ignored (scored nothing) in 2023 because it answers a different question — direction without magnitude. Mg loses two electrons and is also "positive", but its ion is 2+. The charge is a number with a sign: +1, 2+, 3−, written either way round, or as the symbol Na⁺.

questions.promptHtml: Element Y is in Group 8 (the noble gases). How many electrons does it have available for bonding, and what does that predict about its chemistry?
questions.answerHtml:
Zero. A Group 8 element has a full outer shell — no tendency to lose, gain or share anything. (2024's answer line literally accepted "0".)

Prediction: unreactive — noble gases form almost no compounds, exist as single atoms, and are the exam's example of why full shells are the stable end-state that every other atom is scrambling towards by ionic or covalent bonding.

modules.title: Bonding and Structures
modules.standfirst: Three bond types, four structures, and one iron law: properties follow structure. The killer distinction on every paper is bonds versus intermolecular forces — confuse them once in an answer and the whole explanation scores zero.

intel.html:
PaperWhat was asked

2022 Q10 (9)N₂ dot-and-cross; forces in a covalent bond (nuclei, plural!); name diamond from its structure; why C₆₀ fullerene melts far below graphite — 4 marks of structure v bonding

One error dominates this topic, and the schemes kill entire answers for it:

2021: "If any reference to/implication of breaking covalent or ionic bonds scores 0/2" — for why hydrogen's boiling point is low.

2025: the ionic melting-point answer scored 0 marks if it mentioned covalent bonds, molecules, or intermolecular forces.

2022: "Mention of intermolecular forces in graphite: no M2 or M5."

Giant structures have bonds (or ionic/metallic attractions) between particles; simple molecular substances have weak forces between molecules. Pick the right story before writing a word.

subsections.html: Atoms bond three ways: give electrons away (ionic), share them (covalent), or pool them (metallic). But melting points and conductivity are set by the structure — giant or molecular — not by the bond type alone. Structure first, then everything else follows.

subsections.heading: Ionic bonding — transfer, then attraction
subsections.html:
Spec 1.37, 1.40, 1.41 · 2021 Q3c · 2023 Q2a · 2025 Q6b

Metal atoms lose their outer electrons; non-metal atoms gain them. Both end with full outer shells, and the story must be told with numbers:

  • Na (2.8.1) loses one electron → Na⁺ (2.8); Cl (2.8.7) gains one → Cl⁻ (2.8.8).
  • Mg (2.8.2) loses two → Mg²⁺ (2.8); O (2.6) gains two → O²⁻ (2.8).

The 2023 marker: "Needed the idea of 2 electrons to score — several just said electrons moved from magnesium to oxygen without specifying how many." The ionic bond itself is the electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions — attraction, not sharing, and not "the transfer" (the transfer makes the ions; the attraction is the bond).

Formula from charges (2025 Q6b): calcium forms Ca²⁺, phosphorus forms P³⁻ (phosphide); charges must cancel, so 3 × (2+) balances 2 × (3−) → Ca₃P₂. Any mention of sharing in an ionic-formula answer scored zero.

subsections.heading: Covalent bonding — a shared pair pulled by two nuclei
subsections.html:
Spec 1.44, 1.45, 1.46 · 2021 Q2 · 2022 Q10a · 2023 Q4a · 2024 Q3a

A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons. What holds it together: the shared pair is electrostatically attracted to the nuclei of both atoms — and the schemes demand the plural. 2021 and 2022 both refused the mark for "attracted to the nucleus".

Dot-and-cross drill (show outer electrons only): count each atom's outer electrons, give every atom a full shell.

  • HCl: one shared pair; chlorine keeps three lone pairs.
  • NH₃: three N–H pairs; nitrogen keeps one lone pair. (M1 was the three bonding pairs; M2 the rest exactly right.)
  • N₂: a triple bond — six shared electrons — plus one lone pair on each nitrogen.
  • H₂O₂: H–O–O–H — three bonding pairs in a chain, two lone pairs on each oxygen.

Marks are lost to miscounted lone pairs, not to untidy circles — the schemes accept any mix of dots and crosses.

subsections.heading: Simple molecular substances — why strong bonds still boil low
subsections.html:
Spec 1.47, 1.48, 1.51 · 2021 Q2b · 2024 Q9b

H₂, Cl₂, CO₂, water, alkanes: strong covalent bonds inside each molecule, but only weak intermolecular forces between molecules. Boiling separates molecules from each other — it does not break a single covalent bond. So:

The two-mark script for "strong bonds, low boiling point"

1. There are only weak forces of attraction between the molecules (weak intermolecular forces) 1

2. So little energy is needed to overcome them / separate the molecules 1

Any reference to breaking covalent bonds: 0/2. The bonds are bystanders.

Bigger molecules → stronger intermolecular forces → higher boiling points. That is 2024's alkane question: a long-chain hydrocarbon boils higher because the intermolecular forces between its molecules are stronger and need more energy to overcome — forces between molecules, never "between atoms". Covalent substances also do not conduct: no ions, no free electrons.

subsections.heading: Giant structures — ionic, covalent, metallic
subsections.html:
Spec 1.42, 1.43, 1.49, 1.50, 1.52C – 1.54C · 2023 Q6e · 2022 Q10b · 2025 Q4a

Giant ionic lattice (NaCl, MgO): every ion surrounded by opposite charges. High melting point, and the three-mark answer is fixed: giant ionic structure · strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions · lots of energy needed to overcome. Conducts only when molten or dissolved (ions free to move) — never solid, and never by electrons.

Giant covalent (diamond, graphite, SiO₂): millions of atoms covalently bonded in a network. Melting means breaking covalent bonds — here, and only here, that phrase is correct — so melting points are enormous.

  • Diamond: each carbon bonded to 4 others — rigid tetrahedral network → extremely hard, no conduction (no free electrons).
  • Graphite: each carbon bonded to 3 → flat layers with delocalised electrons between them. Layers slide (soft, a lubricant); the delocalised electrons conduct.
  • C₆₀ fullerene: 60 carbons — but a simple molecular structure! Melting C₆₀ overcomes intermolecular forces between the balls, so it melts far below graphite. The 2022 four-marker is precisely this contrast: graphite giant covalent, bonds broken; C₆₀ molecular, IMF overcome; bonds need more energy than IMF.

Giant metallic (2025 Q4a): a lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons — those are the two labels, and "protons" was explicitly rejected. The attraction between ions and electron sea is metallic bonding. Delocalised electrons move → metals conduct; layers of ions slide over each other → malleable (the scheme rejected intermolecular-forces stories here too).

subsections.heading: Diagnosing a mystery substance from its properties
subsections.html:
2021 Q3a

The properties table is a four-way key. Two questions decide everything:

  1. Conducts as a solid? Yes → metal. (Graphite is the exam's favourite exception.)
  2. Conducts only when molten/dissolved? → ionic. Never conducts? Low melting point → simple molecular; huge melting point → giant covalent.

2021's grid: mp −101 °C, never conducts → simple molecular (a gas at 20 °C since bp −35 °C); mp 1063 °C, conducts solid → metal; mp 801 °C, conducts molten only → ionic; mp 3550 °C, never conducts → giant covalent (diamond).

The one distinction everything follows from

Giant structures: strong bonds/attractions are overcome on melting. Simple molecular: weak forces BETWEEN molecules are overcome — the covalent bonds never break. Choose the story before you write; mixing them scores zero.

questions.promptHtml: The H–H bond is one of the strongest single bonds known, yet hydrogen boils at −253 °C. Resolve the contradiction — and explain why "some of the covalent bonds break on boiling" scores 0/2 rather than 1/2.
questions.answerHtml:
No contradiction: boiling and bond-breaking are different events. Boiling only has to separate whole molecules from each other, and between H₂ molecules there are just weak intermolecular forces — very little energy overcomes them, hence −253 °C. The strong H–H bond travels intact inside every molecule of the gas.

It scores 0/2 because the error isn't a missing detail — it is the wrong physical story. An answer built on bond-breaking describes a chemical decomposition, not boiling, so neither marking point is present. That is why the schemes treat one mention of bond-breaking as fatal rather than partial.

questions.promptHtml: Sodium chloride at 801 °C and diamond at 3550 °C both have giant structures. What is being overcome when each one melts, and why is "strong bonds" an incomplete answer for NaCl?
questions.answerHtml:
NaCl: the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions throughout the lattice. The three-marker wants the structure named (giant ionic), the attraction identified (between oppositely charged ions), and the energy statement (a lot needed to overcome it).

Diamond: actual covalent bonds — every carbon is pinned to four others, and melting means breaking that network. This is the one place "bonds break on melting" is the right answer.

"Strong bonds" alone fails for NaCl because it never says what kind of attraction or between what — and worse, it invites covalent language, which zeroes the answer. Name the particles: ions, oppositely charged.

questions.promptHtml: Graphite and C₆₀ fullerene are both pure carbon with covalent bonds. Why does graphite survive to ~3600 °C while C₆₀ melts far lower — and which single word in a student's answer would destroy the graphite half?
questions.answerHtml:
Different structures. Graphite is giant covalent: one continuous network, so melting must break covalent bonds — hugely expensive. C₆₀ is simple molecular: discrete 60-atom balls, held to each other only by weak intermolecular forces; melting just pulls the balls apart and leaves every bond intact. Covalent bonds need far more energy than IMF — that comparison is its own mark.

The destroying word: "intermolecular" anywhere near graphite. Graphite has no molecules, so it can have no intermolecular forces — the 2022 scheme cancelled both graphite marks when they appeared.

questions.promptHtml: Explain why copper conducts electricity as a solid, sodium chloride only when molten, and chlorine never — naming the moving particle in each case.
questions.answerHtml:
Copper: delocalised electrons move through the lattice of positive ions — mobile charge exists already, so the solid conducts.

Sodium chloride: the charge carriers are the ions themselves. Solid: locked in the lattice — no conduction. Molten (or dissolved): ions free to move — conducts. Electrons never enter this story.

Chlorine: neutral molecules, no ions, no delocalised electrons — no charged particle free to move, ever.

Conduction answers live or die on naming the right particle: electrons for metals (and graphite), ions for ionic compounds, nothing for covalent substances.

questions.promptHtml: Use the charges rule to explain why calcium phosphide is Ca₃P₂ and not CaP — and why a sharing-based explanation was awarded zero.
questions.answerHtml:
Calcium (Group 2) forms Ca²⁺; phosphorus (Group 5) gains three electrons to form P³⁻. A formula must be electrically neutral: 2+ and 3− don't cancel one-for-one. The smallest balance is three calciums (6+) against two phosphides (6−) → Ca₃P₂.

Sharing scored zero because this is a metal + non-metal — an ionic compound. Explaining an ionic formula with covalent machinery is the same category error as intermolecular forces in graphite: the wrong model, not a partial answer. Metal + non-metal → transfer and charges, always.

questions.promptHtml: Metals can be hammered into sheets without shattering; ionic crystals crack. Explain both from their structures.
questions.answerHtml:
Metal: the lattice is layers of identical positive ions in a shared electron sea. Hammering makes the layers slide — but every new position looks like the old one: positives still surrounded by the delocalised electrons that bind them. The bonding survives the slide → the metal deforms without breaking (malleable).

Ionic crystal: sliding a layer by one position puts like charges next to each other — positive against positive. Attraction flips to repulsion along the slip plane and the crystal shatters.

For the exam: malleability = layers (of ions) slide over each other — and no intermolecular forces anywhere near this answer (2025 rejected them).

subsections.html: Chemical formulae are not memorised one by one — they are built from ion charges. Equations are then balanced by counting atoms, never by editing formulae. Two rules, endlessly reused.

subsections.heading: The ion charges you must know
subsections.html:
Spec 1.38 · 2024 Q8a

The spec's list, arranged by how you remember it:

  • From the group number: Groups 1, 2, 3 → +1, +2, +3 (Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺). Groups 5, 6, 7 → −3, −2, −1 (N³⁻, O²⁻, Cl⁻).
  • Named metals the table can't tell you: Ag⁺, Zn²⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, Pb²⁺ — silver is +1, zinc always +2, iron comes in two flavours (the Roman numeral in the name says which: iron(III) = Fe³⁺).
  • The molecular ions: H⁺, OH⁻ (hydroxide), NH₄⁺ (ammonium), NO₃⁻ (nitrate), CO₃²⁻ (carbonate), SO₄²⁻ (sulfate).

subsections.heading: Building a formula: charges must cancel
subsections.html:
Spec 1.39 · 2023 Q4b · 2024 Q8a · 2025 Q6b

Total positive charge = total negative charge. The crossing trick: each ion's charge number becomes the other ion's subscript.

  • Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl (1:1, nothing to write).
  • Mg²⁺ + Cl⁻ → MgCl₂; Mg²⁺ + N³⁻ → Mg₃N₂ (2024's table answers).
  • NH₄⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → (NH₄)₂CO₃ — brackets around a molecular ion whenever it is multiplied; (NH₄)₂SO₄ likewise.

Naming runs backwards: MgO = magnesium oxide (spelling counts); NH₄Cl = ammonium chloride. -ide = just the element; -ate = element + oxygen (sulfate, nitrate, carbonate).

Elements that go around in pairs: the diatomic molecules H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂. In any equation, elemental hydrogen is H₂, chlorine Cl₂ — writing a lone Cl was 2023's "fascinating variations" complaint at the electrodes, and it is wrong everywhere else too.

subsections.heading: Balancing: change the big numbers, never the formulae
subsections.html:
Spec 1.25 · 2024 Q5a · 2025 Q4b, Q6d · 2023 Q9b

A chemical equation is an atom ledger — same count of every element on both sides. The method:

  1. Write correct formulae first. These are now frozen — balancing never edits a subscript, only the coefficients in front.
  2. Count each element, fix imbalances one element at a time, recount after each change. Save lone elements (O₂, C) for last — their coefficient can be set freely.
  3. Check the whole thing once more. Half the "did not include balancing numbers" losses are equations abandoned one step early.

The school's set pieces: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO · 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe · 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO₂ · Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 8C → Ca₃P₂ + 8CO (count the oxygens: 8 on each side) · Ca₃P₂ + 6H₂O → 3Ca(OH)₂ + 2PH₃ · ethane's combustion 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. Schemes usually give M1 for formulae, M2 for balancing — and "ALLOW multiples", so doubling everything is fine; fractions usually accepted too.

subsections.heading: State symbols — and which one is the actual test
subsections.html:
Spec 1.25 · 2021 Q8a · 2022 Q3b · 2024 Q10a · 2025 Q4b

(s) solid · (l) pure liquid · (g) gas · (aq) dissolved in water. The papers' favourite: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).

Three decisions carry the marks:

  • Water is (l) — it is the liquid itself, not dissolved in anything.
  • Acids and dissolved salts are (aq) — 2024's commentary: many wrote zinc nitrate as (s) or (l); it is a soluble salt in solution. Check the solubility rules when unsure.
  • Precipitates are (s) — insoluble products are solid even though they formed in solution: Al(OH)₃(s), PbBr₂(s).

The two rules everything follows from

Formulae: charges cancel. Equations: atoms balance — adjust coefficients, never subscripts.

questions.promptHtml: Why is magnesium chloride MgCl₂ but sodium chloride just NaCl? Explain from the charges, and state what the "crossing trick" is actually doing.
questions.answerHtml:
Compounds are electrically neutral. Mg²⁺ carries two positives, and each Cl⁻ only one negative — so it takes two chloride ions to cancel one magnesium: MgCl₂. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ cancel one-for-one: NaCl.

The crossing trick (charge of one ion becomes subscript of the other) is just solving that neutrality equation quickly: it finds the smallest counts that make total + equal total −. That is why the result must always be simplified (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ "cross" to Mg₂O₂ → reduce to MgO).

questions.promptHtml: A student balances Mg + O₂ → MgO by rewriting it as Mg + O₂ → MgO₂. Chemically, what has the student done wrong — and what is the legal fix?
questions.answerHtml:
They have invented a different substance. MgO₂ is not magnesium oxide — the formula of a compound is fixed by its ion charges (Mg²⁺, O²⁻ → MgO) and is not negotiable during balancing. Editing subscripts changes what reacts, not how much.

The legal fix uses coefficients only: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO — four atoms of magnesium-and-oxygen on each side, formulae untouched. (With state symbols, 2025's version: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s).)

questions.promptHtml: In Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 8C → Ca₃P₂ + 8CO, show the oxygen audit that makes 8 the right coefficient for both carbon and CO.
questions.answerHtml:
Left side oxygen: (PO₄)₂ = 2 × 4 = 8 oxygens. Calcium (3) and phosphorus (2) already match Ca₃P₂ — so all 8 oxygens must leave inside CO, one each: 8CO. Eight CO needs eight carbons: 8C.

Recount: Ca 3=3, P 2=2, O 8=8, C 8=8. ✓ The general skill: brackets multiply everything inside, and a systematic per-element count beats staring. This equation appeared two years running (2024, 2025) — the school likes it because the bracket-counting is the whole test.

questions.promptHtml: The same reaction — zinc + nitric acid → zinc nitrate + hydrogen — gets four state symbols. Give them, and explain the two that students got wrong in 2024.
questions.answerHtml:
Zn(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Zn(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂(g).

The two casualties: zinc nitrate, widely written (s) or (l). It is a soluble salt (all nitrates are soluble) sitting dissolved in the solution it formed in — (aq). It only becomes (s) after you deliberately crystallise it. And the acid: dilute acid is a solution, always (aq), never (l).

The habit: for every substance ask where is it, physically, in the flask? — not what it could be in a bottle somewhere.

questions.promptHtml: Ammonia reacts with sulfuric acid to give ammonium sulfate. Build the product's formula from its ions, then write and balance the full equation.
questions.answerHtml:
Formula: NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻ — two ammoniums cancel one sulfate → (NH₄)₂SO₄, brackets because the molecular ion is doubled.

Equation: the product contains two NH₄ groups, so two ammonia molecules are needed: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄. Count: N 2=2, H (6+2)=8=8, S 1=1, O 4=4. ✓

(2023 asked exactly this; state symbols were ignored even if wrong there — but the balancing 2 was required.)

subsections.html: An acid in water releases H⁺ ions; an alkali releases OH⁻. Everything else — indicators, neutralisation, the three salt preparations — is bookkeeping about where those ions and their partners end up.

subsections.heading: Acids, alkalis and the pH scale
subsections.html:
Spec 2.28 – 2.33 · 2021 Q1 · 2022 Q1

Acids (HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃) are a source of hydrogen ions, H⁺, in solution. Alkalis (NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)₂) are a source of hydroxide ions, OH⁻. The pH scale runs 0–14: 0–3 strongly acidic, 4–6 weakly acidic, 7 neutral, 8–10 weakly alkaline, 11–14 strongly alkaline.

The three indicators the spec names, with their exam colours:

  • Litmus: red in acid, blue in alkali (purple neutral).
  • Phenolphthalein: colourless in acid, pink in alkali.
  • Methyl orange: red in acid, yellow in alkali.

Universal indicator gives the approximate pH by colour sweep (red → green at 7 → purple). To show a solution is acidic: blue litmus turns red — say the change, not just the final colour.

In the proton language the spec asks for: an acid is a proton donor, a base a proton acceptor — neutralisation is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, a proton handed over.

subsections.heading: Bases, alkalis, and the reactions that make salts
subsections.html:
Spec 2.37, 2.38 · 2022 Q1d · 2024 Q10a

A base is any metal oxide, metal hydroxide or ammonia; an alkali is a base that dissolves in water. The salt-forming reactions, each with its giveaway observation:

  • acid + metal → salt + hydrogen — effervescence, metal disappears. (Nitric acid + metals is excluded from the spec — use Mg or Zn with HCl or H₂SO₄ in answers you invent.)
  • acid + base (oxide/hydroxide) → salt + water — the classic neutralisation.
  • acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide — effervescence, gas turns limewater milky.

Which salt? The acid decides the surname: hydrochloric → chlorides, sulfuric → sulfates, nitric → nitrates. HCl + KOH → potassium chloride + water.

Observation questions: say what your eyes see — effervescence/bubbles, the solid disappears, a colour change. "Hydrogen is given off" is a deduction, not an observation, and the schemes ignore it. 2021 also rejected extra wrong observations bolted on ("white flame") — do not decorate.

subsections.heading: The solubility rules — the map that picks the method
subsections.html:
Spec 2.34 · 2022 Q7a · 2024 Q2b

Learn these six lines; every salt question starts by consulting them:

  • All sodium, potassium and ammonium salts — soluble. ("Sodium salts are always soluble" — the 2025 marker, twice.)
  • All nitrates — soluble.
  • Chlorides — soluble, except silver and lead(II).
  • Sulfates — soluble, except barium, calcium and lead(II).
  • Carbonates — insoluble, except sodium, potassium, ammonium.
  • Hydroxides — insoluble, except sodium, potassium (calcium slightly).

The "which pair precipitates?" MCQ is just cross-checking: potassium carbonate + calcium nitrate → potassium nitrate (soluble) and calcium carbonate (insoluble — precipitate!). Sodium chloride + ammonium nitrate → both products soluble → nothing happens.

subsections.heading: Method 1 — soluble salt from an acid + excess insoluble solid
subsections.html:
Spec 2.39 · 2024 Q10b · 2021 Q5a

For salts of Mg, Zn, Cu… : react the acid with an excess of the insoluble metal, oxide or carbonate.

  1. Add the solid to the acid until it is in excess — so that all the acid is used up (that is the reason the schemes want).
  2. Filter off the excess solid.
  3. Heat the filtrate until the crystallisation point (crystals just start to form / a saturated solution) — never to dryness.
  4. Leave to cool and crystallise.
  5. Pour off / filter the remaining liquid, and dry the crystals with a named method: pat with filter paper, leave in a warm place or a (warm) oven.

The two killers, straight from the schemes: heating to dryness collapses the answer to 1 mark (it destroys hydrated crystals — the water of crystallisation is boiled away, and for some salts the salt decomposes); and "leave the crystals to dry" without a method was refused the final mark in 2024 — name how.

subsections.heading: Method 2 — soluble salt from an acid + alkali (titration route)
subsections.html:
Spec 2.40C · 2025 Q2a

When both reactants are soluble (sodium, potassium, ammonium salts), there is no excess solid to filter: use an indicator to find the exact neutralisation volume, then repeat with the same volumes without the indicator (or remove it with charcoal), and crystallise as before: heat to the crystallisation point, cool, decant, dry.

2025 asked only for the crystallisation half — and the marks were exactly: heat to crystallisation point · cool to crystallise · pour off excess liquid · dry in a warm place. Adding any new chemical at this stage scored zero: the solution already contains only the salt and water.

subsections.heading: Method 3 — insoluble salt by precipitation (mix, filter, wash, dry)
subsections.html:
Spec 2.41C · 2022 Q7b · 2023 Q10 · 2025 Q7a

For BaSO₄, PbBr₂, AgCl, Cu(OH)₂…: mix two solutions that each carry half of the target — lead(II) nitrate + sodium bromide → PbBr₂↓ + sodium nitrate (both parents chosen soluble; nitrates and sodium salts always are).

  1. Mix the two solutions — the schemes reject mixing solids.
  2. Filter — the salt you want is the residue on the paper.
  3. Wash the residue with distilled water — rinses away the soluble by-product clinging to it.
  4. Dry — filter paper, warm oven, leave to dry. No direct heating with a Bunsen (2022 rejected it).

Wrong-method answers are the biggest single loss on salt questions. Describing the excess-base method for a precipitation scored 1 of 4 in 2025 and 1 of 3 in 2023. And it is the residue that is washed and dried — 2023's marker: "the salt you want is the residue", not the filtrate. If the product is insoluble, there is no crystallisation step anywhere.

subsections.heading: Choosing the method — the ten-second decision
subsections.html:
every salt question

  1. Is the target salt insoluble? (check the rules) → Method 3: mix solutions, filter, wash residue, dry.
  2. Soluble, and the partner solid is insoluble (metal/oxide/carbonate)? → Method 1: excess solid, filter, crystallise.
  3. Soluble, and both reactants soluble (Na/K/NH₄ salt from acid + alkali)? → Method 2: titrate, then crystallise.

2021's find-the-mistake question was this decision in disguise: nitric acid can't make a sulfate; magnesium carbonate is insoluble so there is no "solution of magnesium carbonate"; and boiling to dryness wrecks the hydrated crystals.

The one decision everything follows from

Look up the solubility first. Insoluble target → precipitate, filter, wash the residue, dry. Soluble target → make a solution of just salt + water, then heat only to the crystallisation point — never to dryness.

questions.promptHtml: Why does the soluble-salt method demand an excess of the solid, when excess sounds wasteful — and how does the excess then leave the story?
questions.answerHtml:
The excess guarantees that all the acid has reacted. If any acid survived, it would stay dissolved in the filtrate and end up concentrated in your crystals — the product would be contaminated with acid you cannot see.

An excess of an insoluble solid is trivially removed: filter it off. That is the whole design of the method — the impurity you deliberately created is the one impurity filtering can remove. (2024's one-marker: "so that all the nitric acid reacts". "To make more salt" misses the logic entirely.)

questions.promptHtml: Heating the filtrate "until crystals just start to form" and then stopping feels unfinished. Why is stopping there exactly right, and what goes wrong for a hydrated salt if you keep heating to dryness?
questions.answerHtml:
Stopping at the crystallisation point leaves a hot saturated solution. As it cools, solubility falls and the salt comes out of solution slowly as well-formed crystals, leaving the remaining impurities behind in the liquid you then pour off.

Boiling to dryness does the opposite: everything in the solution — impurities included — is baked onto the dish, and for a hydrated salt the heat also drives off the water of crystallisation, so you get a powdery anhydrous solid (or a decomposed one) instead of the hydrated crystals the question asked for. That is why every scheme caps a heated-to-dryness answer at 1 mark.

questions.promptHtml: In the precipitation method, what exactly does washing the residue with distilled water remove — and why does washing the filtrate instead earn the 2023 marker's special scorn?
questions.answerHtml:
The precipitate on the filter paper is soaked in the reaction mixture, which contains the soluble by-product (sodium nitrate, in the PbBr₂ preparation) and any unreacted solutions. A rinse of distilled water dissolves those away; the insoluble product itself cannot dissolve, so it stays put — the wash purifies for free.

The filtrate is the liquid that passed through: by-product solution. Washing it is washing the waste. The confusion comes from Method 1, where the filtrate is the valuable part — which is exactly why the papers keep asking both: they are testing whether you know which side of the filter paper your product is on. Insoluble product → residue; soluble product → filtrate.

questions.promptHtml: Silver chloride is insoluble. A student proposes making it by adding excess silver to hydrochloric acid, then filtering. Give two separate reasons the plan fails, and the correct recipe.
questions.answerHtml:
Reason 1 — wrong method for the product: even if the reaction worked, an insoluble product forms wherever it is made — mixed in with the excess solid — and filtering would collect both together. The excess-solid method only works when the product stays dissolved.

Reason 2 — the reaction doesn't go: silver is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it does not react with dilute acids at all.

Correct recipe: precipitation from two soluble parents — silver nitrate solution + sodium chloride solution (nitrates always soluble, sodium salts always soluble) → AgCl precipitates → filter, wash the residue, dry.

questions.promptHtml: Copper sulfate solution is mixed with sodium hydroxide solution. State what you would SEE, name both products, and explain which preparation method this reaction belongs to.
questions.answerHtml:
Seen: a blue precipitate/solid forms (and the blue solution fades). Not "crystals", not "fizzing" — nothing here makes a gas, and 2023 rejected fizzing outright.

Products: copper(II) hydroxide (the blue precipitate — hydroxides are insoluble except Na/K) and sodium sulfate (stays dissolved — sodium salts always soluble).

Method: precipitation (Method 3): filter, wash the residue, dry gently. The question told you a precipitate formed; answers describing excess-base-and-crystallise were the standard way to lose all three method marks.

questions.promptHtml: Aluminium sulfate is used by gardeners to acidify soil: Al₂(SO₄)₃(s) + 6H₂O(l) → 2Al(OH)₃(s) + 3H₂SO₄(aq). Using only the state symbols, explain why the products make the soil acidic and not neutral.
questions.answerHtml:
Both an acid and a base are produced — but their states differ. Al(OH)₃ is (s): solid, insoluble, so its OH⁻ ions are locked away and never enter the soil water. H₂SO₄ is (aq): dissolved, so its H⁺ ions are released into solution.

Free H⁺ with no free OH⁻ to cancel it → the soil water is acidic. The general lesson (it earned both marks in 2021): ions only count when they are in solution — (s) means chemically present but unavailable.

subsections.html: Every calculation on these papers is the same three-step journey: grams → moles → whatever was asked (grams of something else, a volume of gas, a formula, a yield). The mole is the bridge in the middle; the balanced equation is the exchange rate.

subsections.heading: The mole, and the one equation that runs the topic
subsections.html:
Spec 1.27, 1.28 · every paper

A mole is just a counted amount of particles — 6.0 × 10²³ of them. Its usefulness: one mole of anything weighs its Mr in grams. So:

n = mass ÷ Mr — and rearranged, mass = n × Mr.

Mr (relative formula mass) is the sum of the Ar values from the periodic table: Na₂CO₃ = (2 × 23) + 12 + (3 × 16) = 106. Brackets multiply everything inside: Ca(OH)₂ = 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74.

2024 extended this to counting particles: 0.081 g of H₂ = 0.081 ÷ 2 = 0.0405 mol → 0.0405 × 6.0 × 10²³ = 2.4 × 10²² molecules (2 sf, standard form — both were demanded).

subsections.heading: Using the balanced equation as an exchange rate
subsections.html:
Spec 1.29 · 2021 Q6 · 2024 Q3e

The big numbers in a balanced equation are mole ratios. The routine, always in this order:

  1. Moles of what you know: 10.5 g NaHCO₃ ÷ 84 = 0.125 mol
  2. Ratio across the equation: 2NaHCO₃ → CO₂, so ÷2 → 0.0625 mol CO₂
  3. Convert to what was asked: mass 0.0625 × 44 = 2.75 g, or volume 0.0625 × 24,000 = 1500 cm³

Ratios also settle excess questions (2025: 1.5 g Mg = 0.0625 mol needs 0.125 mol of acid, only 0.1 mol present, so the magnesium is in excess) — always compare moles needed against moles available, never masses.

subsections.heading: Gas volumes — the molar volume shortcut
subsections.html:
Spec 1.35C · 2022 Q8 · 2023 Q6 · 2024 Q3e · 2025 Q3a

One mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure occupies 24 dm³ = 24,000 cm³. So volume = moles × 24 (in dm³), and moles = volume ÷ 24,000 (in cm³). Match the unit to the one printed on the answer line before you calculate.

The school's set-piece (used in 2022 and re-used in 2023): 6.4 tonnes of sulfur → SO₂. 6.4 × 10⁶ g ÷ 32 = 2.0 × 10⁵ mol → × 24 = 4.8 × 10⁶ dm³, in standard form — the third mark was literally for writing it in standard form.

subsections.heading: Empirical and molecular formulae
subsections.html:
Spec 1.31, 1.32, 1.33 · 2021 Q10a · 2022 Q9 · 2024 Q7 · 2025 Q10

The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. From masses or percentages, the drill is fixed:

  1. Divide each element's mass (or %) by its Ar — from the periodic table, the bigger number, never the atomic number.
  2. Divide everything by the smallest to get the ratio.
  3. If the ratio isn't whole (1 : 1.33), multiply up (× 3 → 3 : 4 → Pb₃O₄) — never round 1.33 to 1.

The molecular formula is a whole multiple of the empirical one: divide the given Mr by the empirical mass. 2022: C₂H₄Cl has empirical mass 63.5; Mr = 127; 127 ÷ 63.5 = 2 → C₄H₈Cl₂.

2021's scheme: "Division by atomic numbers or other inappropriate numbers scores 0/3. Fractions upside down scores 0/3." If your first step is % ÷ Ar you are safe; anything else scores nothing at all.

subsections.heading: Formulae from experiments — the two set practicals
subsections.html:
Spec 1.31, 1.36 (practical) · 2024 Q5b, Q7 · 2021 Q7 · 2022 Q6

Metal oxide by combustion (MgO): weigh crucible empty, with magnesium, and after heating. The gain in mass is the oxygen that combined. The lid is lifted occasionally to let oxygen in; the result improves by reheating and reweighing to constant mass — constant mass is the evidence the reaction (or the drying) is complete.

Metal oxide by reduction (CuO): pass methane/hydrogen over heated oxide; mass falls as oxygen is removed. Mass of metal and mass of oxygen lost → divide each by Ar → ratio (2024: 0.06 : 0.06 = 1 : 1 → CuO).

Water of crystallisation (the crucible/tube practical): hydrated crystals are heated to constant mass. Mass after = anhydrous salt; the loss = water. Then:

  1. moles of anhydrous salt = mass ÷ Mr (2022: 3.18 ÷ 106 = 0.03)
  2. moles of water = mass ÷ 18 (3.78 ÷ 18 = 0.21)
  3. divide by the smaller → 1 : 7 → Na₂CO₃·7H₂O

Every year's twist: why might x come out too low? — not heated long enough, so not all the water was removed. Improve it? — repeat heating to constant mass.

subsections.heading: Ar from isotopes, and percentage yield
subsections.html:
Spec 1.17, 1.30 · 2023 Q9a · 2025 Q7b

Relative atomic mass from abundances is a weighted mean: Ar = Σ(isotope mass × %) ÷ 100. Copper: (63 × 69.5 + 65 × 30.5) ÷ 100 = 63.61 → 63.6 to 3 sf.

Percentage yield = actual mass obtained ÷ theoretical mass × 100. The theoretical mass always comes from a moles calculation: 2025 gave 0.150 mol of PbBr₂ expected → 0.150 × 367 = 55.05 g theoretical; actual 49.6 g → 49.6 ÷ 55.05 × 100 = 90.1%. The scheme explicitly rejected dividing the actual mass by the moles figure — masses over masses, always.

Percentage by mass of an element (2023 Q6c): (atoms × Ar ÷ Mr) × 100 — nitrogen in (NH₄)₂SO₄ = (2 × 14 ÷ 132) × 100 = 21.2%. Count every atom of the element: the 2 outside the bracket doubles the N.

The one journey every question takes

grams → moles → (ratio) → moles → answer. If you are stuck, calculate moles of whatever you were given — it is almost always the first mark.

questions.promptHtml: Why does one mole of CO₂ (44 g) and one mole of H₂ (2 g) — wildly different masses — occupy exactly the same volume as gases at room temperature and pressure?
questions.answerHtml:
Because in a gas the particles are so far apart that the volume is almost entirely empty space — the size and mass of the individual molecules barely matter. What sets the volume is the number of particles (and the temperature and pressure), and one mole of anything is the same number of particles: 6.0 × 10²³.

That is the entire justification for the molar volume shortcut: equal moles of any gas → equal volumes → 24 dm³ per mole at rtp. It works for gases only; solids and liquids have their particles touching, so their volumes depend on what they are.

questions.promptHtml: The empirical drill says "divide the percentage by the Ar". What is that step actually calculating, and why does dividing by the atomic number score zero?
questions.answerHtml:
It converts a mass ratio into a mole ratio — % of mass ÷ mass-per-mole = relative number of moles of atoms. In 100 g of the lead oxide, 90.7 g ÷ 207 g/mol = 0.438 mol of lead atoms. A formula is a ratio of atoms counted, not of grams, so you must get to moles before comparing.

The atomic number is the count of protons — nothing to do with mass. Dividing by it produces a number with no meaning, which is why the scheme kills the whole question (0/3) rather than just one mark: the method itself is wrong, not the arithmetic.

questions.promptHtml: In the water-of-crystallisation practical, the value of x comes out too low even though every weighing was accurate. What happened, how would you detect it, and how do you fix it?
questions.answerHtml:
What happened: the crystals were not heated for long enough, so not all the water of crystallisation was driven off. Some water is still in the "anhydrous" mass, making the salt look heavier and the water lighter — the ratio of water to salt shrinks, so x shrinks.

Detection and fix are the same idea: heat again, cool, reweigh — and repeat until the mass no longer changes. Constant mass is the proof that all the water is gone; a mass still falling means there was more water to lose.

The trap in reverse: if the question says x came out too HIGH, look for the salt decomposing or spitting out of the crucible — mass lost that wasn't water.

questions.promptHtml: A question gives you 1.5 g of magnesium and 0.1 mol of hydrochloric acid, and asks you to "show that the magnesium is in excess" (Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂). Why can't you just compare 1.5 g with the acid's mass — and what is the correct comparison?
questions.answerHtml:
Grams of different substances aren't comparable — a gram of magnesium contains a different number of particles from a gram of HCl, and the equation trades in particles, not grams.

The correct route: 1.5 ÷ 24 = 0.0625 mol Mg. The ratio is 1 : 2, so reacting all of it needs 2 × 0.0625 = 0.125 mol of acid. Only 0.1 mol is available — the acid runs out first, so the magnesium is in excess.

The template for every excess/"show that" question: moles of both → scale one by the ratio → compare needed vs available, in moles.

questions.promptHtml: Why is the percentage yield of a real preparation always less than 100% — and why does the exam's yield formula use two masses rather than two amounts in moles?
questions.answerHtml:
Less than 100%: product is physically lost at every step — some stays dissolved in the solution after crystallisation, some is left on the filter paper or washed away, side reactions consume reactant. (In 2025's PbBr₂ preparation, ~10% went missing largely in filtering and washing.)

Why masses: actual ÷ theoretical is only meaningful when both are the same kind of quantity. You weigh the actual product, so the theoretical value must be converted all the way to a mass (moles expected × Mr) before dividing. The 2025 scheme specifically rejected 49.6 ÷ 0.150 — a mass divided by an amount of moles is a nonsense number.

questions.promptHtml: Chlorine's Ar is 35.5 — not a whole number, though every single chlorine atom has a whole-number mass. Explain, and state what a 75% ³⁵Cl / 25% ³⁷Cl mixture gives.
questions.answerHtml:
Ar is a weighted average over the isotopes as they occur naturally, not the mass of any one atom. Individual atoms are ³⁵Cl or ³⁷Cl; the average of a big natural sample sits in between, pulled towards the more abundant one.

(35 × 75 + 37 × 25) ÷ 100 = (2625 + 925) ÷ 100 = 35.5.

Sanity check that catches sign-of-life errors: the answer must lie between the isotope masses, nearer the more abundant isotope. 2023's copper answer (63.6, close to 63 at 69.5%) passes exactly that check.

questions.promptHtml: 2023 gave a solid metal carbonate XCO₃ that decomposed to give 0.05 mol of CO₂ from 7.40 g. Walk the route from those two numbers to the identity of X, and say where the periodic table enters.
questions.answerHtml:
Three steps, each one mark:

  1. Ratio: XCO₃ → XO + CO₂ is 1 : 1, so moles of XCO₃ = moles of CO₂ = 0.05.
  2. Mr from the definition of moles: Mr = mass ÷ n = 7.40 ÷ 0.05 = 148.
  3. Subtract the known part: CO₃ contributes 60, so Ar(X) = 148 − 60 = 88. The periodic table's Group 2 metal with Ar 88 is strontium.

This is the pattern for every identify-the-element question: get moles, get Mr, strip away what you know, look up what remains — using the question's own constraint (a Group 2 metal) to pick the match.

subsections.html: Solubility is a number with strict units: how many grams of solute saturate 100 g of water at a given temperature. The whole topic is that sentence plus a graph of how the number changes with temperature.

subsections.heading: The four words, exactly
subsections.html:
Spec 1.4

The solute is the solid that dissolves; the solvent is the liquid doing the dissolving; together they make a solution. A solution is saturated when no more solute will dissolve at that temperature — the phrase "at that temperature" carries the mark, because a saturated solution at 70 °C is an unsaturated one at 80 °C.

What affects how much dissolves? Temperature (the examinable factor — 2024's answer), plus the choice of solvent and, of course, how much solvent you have. Stirring and crushing change the speed of dissolving, never the amount — the schemes explicitly ignore them.

subsections.heading: Solubility curves — reading them without losing marks
subsections.html:
Spec 1.5C, 1.6C · 2022 Q4 · 2023 Q12 · 2025 Q5

A solubility curve plots g per 100 g of water against temperature; for most solids it rises. Each point on the curve reads: "a saturated solution at this temperature holds this much." The three set-piece readings:

  • Where are two solubilities equal? Where the curves cross. Draw the vertical line down from the crossing and show it — the answer without the construction line lost a mark in both 2023 and 2025.
  • How much dissolves in some other amount of water? Scale linearly: 124 g per 100 g means 124 × 2.5 = 310 g per 250 g. If the data is "per 25 cm³", multiply by 4 for per 100 g — 1 cm³ of water has a mass of 1 g, so cm³ of water and g of water are the same number.
  • Read the curve the question names. Two curves are printed precisely so you can grab the wrong one under time pressure — 2023's most common error.

subsections.heading: Cooling a saturated solution — where the crystals come from
subsections.html:
Spec 1.6C · 2023 Q12b · 2024 Q2c · 2025 Q5d

Cool a saturated solution and the water can hold less; the surplus crystallises out. The mass of crystals is a subtraction of two curve readings:

The two-read subtraction

1. Solubility at the hot temperature (read the curve, show the lines) 1

2. Solubility at the cold temperature, subtract: mass crystallising per 100 g = hot − cold 1

2023: 45 − 13 = 32 g. If the solution used 250 g of water, scale the answer by 2.5 at the end.

This is the quantitative version of the crystallisation step in salt preparation: heat to saturation, cool, and the falling curve hands you crystals.

subsections.heading: Measuring solubility — the evaporating-basin method
subsections.html:
Spec 1.7 (practical) · 2024 Q2d

The school's method, in the order the flowchart question wants:

  1. Put a known volume of water in a beaker; add solute a little at a time, stirring, until no more dissolves (some solid remains — the solution is saturated).
  2. Filter to obtain a measured volume of the clear saturated solution.
  3. Weigh an empty evaporating basin; add the solution and weigh again.
  4. Gently heat to evaporate all the water, then weigh the basin with the dry salt.

Mass of salt = (basin + dry salt) − (empty basin); scale to 100 g of water. 2024's numbers: 78.2 − 50.5 = 27.7 g from 50 cm³ of water → × 2 = 55.4 g per 100 g.

Two subtleties the papers have asked: values measured near 100 °C are less accurate because water evaporates while you work (2022); and yes — here you do evaporate to dryness, because the product being weighed is the total dissolved salt, not nice hydrated crystals. Purpose decides the technique.

The one number everything follows from

Solubility = grams of solute that saturate 100 g of water at a stated temperature. Every question is reading, scaling, or subtracting that number.

questions.promptHtml: A saturated solution of KNO₃ at 70 °C sits in an open beaker overnight and cools to 20 °C. Describe everything that is different in the morning, with the reasoning.
questions.answerHtml:
Crystals of KNO₃ now sit at the bottom. At 70 °C the water held the full 70-degree solubility; at 20 °C it can hold far less. The surplus had nowhere to go but out of solution — it crystallised.

The remaining liquid is still saturated — but at 20 °C, holding the 20-degree amount. The mass of crystals = (solubility at 70°) − (solubility at 20°), scaled to the actual mass of water. That subtraction is the exam question, every year.

questions.promptHtml: 2025's table gave the mass dissolving in 25 cm³ of water, and the answer line demanded "g per 100 g of water". What conversion is needed, and why does the question feel entitled to swap between cm³ and g of water without comment?
questions.answerHtml:
Multiply the reading by 4 — four lots of 25 make 100.

The silent swap works because 1.00 cm³ of water has a mass of 1.00 g — the density of water is the one conversion factor the papers assume without stating (2024 printed it as a hint; 2025 didn't). So 25 cm³ of water is 25 g of water, and volume-of-water numbers slot straight into solubility units.

It only works for water — never apply it to another liquid or to the solution itself.

questions.promptHtml: Why are solubility values measured at 95 °C systematically less accurate than those at 25 °C — and is the error high or low?
questions.answerHtml:
Near boiling, the water evaporates significantly while the measurement is being made. Less water is present than you think.

The same mass of dissolved salt sitting in less water than recorded means the calculated "per 100 g" figure comes out too high — the salt gets credited to water that has already left. (The one-mark exam answer is just "water evaporates"; the direction of the error is the understanding behind it.)

questions.promptHtml: In the evaporating-basin practical you heat to complete dryness — the exact step the salt-preparation module forbids. Why is it right here and wrong there?
questions.answerHtml:
Different goal, different technique. Here the product is a number: the total mass of dissolved salt. Boiling everything off and weighing the solid residue measures exactly that — you want every last gram out of solution, and you don't care what state the crystals are in.

In salt preparation the product is the substance: well-formed, hydrated crystals. There, heating to dryness wrecks the crystals and drives off the water of crystallisation.

If an exam answer needs one sentence: evaporate to dryness to measure solubility; heat only to the crystallisation point to prepare crystals.

questions.promptHtml: Two curves cross at 68 °C. A student answers "at 68 °C the solutions are the same" and scores one mark of two. What exactly did the second mark want?
questions.answerHtml:
The construction line on the graph. The schemes in 2023, 2024 and 2025 all award a mark for the visible working: the vertical line dropped from the crossing point (or lines to the axes for any reading).

The habit that banks these marks: for any value read from a graph, rule the lines first, read second, and leave the lines on the paper. It also silently protects you — an answer read from the wrong place with lines shown can still earn the method mark.

subsections.html: Rate is about how fast a reaction goes — never how much product it makes. Everything in this topic is one idea (particles must collide, hard enough, often enough) applied to five factors and read off two kinds of graph.

subsections.heading: What rate means, and the three ways it is measured
subsections.html:
Spec 3.9 · 2021 Q8 · 2022 Q3 · 2023 Q7

Rate = how much reactant is used up, or product is made, per unit time. The school's papers measure it three ways:

  • Mass loss on a balance — marble chips + hydrochloric acid in a flask with a cotton wool plug. The CO₂ escapes, so the reading falls. The plug stops acid spray escaping so the mass decrease is only due to the gas — it must still let the gas out.
  • Gas collected in a syringe — magnesium + acid, or hydrogen peroxide decomposing. Volume rises with time.
  • Time for a change to happen — in the booklet practicals: time to collect a set volume, or for a cross to disappear.

2022 asked why the cotton wool increases accuracy, and the mark scheme rejected "it stops the gas escaping" — the gas must escape or the mass would not change. The answer is that it stops acid splashing out, so the mass decrease is due to the gas alone.

subsections.heading: The graph is the question: reading rate curves
subsections.html:
Spec 3.9 · 2023 Q7 · 2025 Q1

Amount of product against time gives the same curve every year:

  • Steepest at the start — reactant concentration is highest, so collisions are most frequent.
  • Flattens as reactant is used up — collisions become less frequent.
  • Horizontal when the reaction has finished — one reactant is completely used up. On a total-mass graph this appears as a falling curve that levels off.

Two set-piece tasks come with the graph, and both have exact rules:

Reading a value: draw a vertical line from the time up to the curve and across to the axis — and show those lines. 2023: "They had to show working-out lines on graph to get the full 2 marks."

Rate at an instant (tangent): draw a tangent touching the curve at that time only, make a large triangle, rate = change in y ÷ change in x, and give the unit the axes demand: cm³/min, g/s. The four marks in 2025 were exactly: tangent drawn · triangle measurements · gradient calculation · correct unit.

Rate at 60 s means the tangent gradient at 60 s, not total change ÷ 60. In 2022 the average-rate answer scored 1 of 3. And the average rate over the first minute is a different number from the rate at 60 s — the curve is always slowing.

subsections.heading: Collision theory — the three-mark answer that is always the same
subsections.html:
Spec 3.10, 3.11 · every paper 2021–2025

Particles react only when they collide with energy at or above the activation energy. Every factor question is answered by saying what happens to the frequency of successful collisions:

The template

1. What changed about the particles (more per volume / more energy / more exposed surface) 1

2. The word successful and/or energy ≥ activation energy where temperature is involved 1

3. Collisions happen more frequently / more per unit time → rate increases 1

  • Concentration ↑ (or gas pressure ↑): more particles in the same volume → more frequent collisions. Never mention energy here — 2024's scheme capped the answer at 1 mark if kinetic energy appeared in a concentration answer.
  • Temperature ↑: particles have more (kinetic) energy → more collisions have energy above the activation energy (a greater proportion are successful) → and collisions are more frequent. 2023: "They had to say that more/a greater proportion of collisions are successful. Too many merged this point with collision frequency."
  • Surface area ↑ (powder instead of chips/ribbon): more particles exposed → more frequent collisions. Total amount is unchanged, so the final amount of product is unchanged — the plateau is reached sooner but at the same height.
  • Catalyst: see below.

Say the concentration of the acid, not "the concentration of magnesium" — 2023's marker penalised that exact phrase. Solids do not have a concentration.

subsections.heading: Catalysts — both halves or no mark
subsections.html:
Spec 3.12, 3.13 · 2024 Q3 · 2025 Q1

A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate without being chemically changed or used up. How it works is a fixed two-marker:

The two-mark script for "explain how a catalyst increases rate"

1. It provides an alternative reaction pathway 1

2. …with a lower activation energy 1

So a greater proportion of collisions are successful. Saying only "it lowers the activation energy" was the standard way to drop a mark in 2025 — the pathway is the mechanism, the lower Eₐ is the consequence.

The school's example is always manganese(IV) oxide catalysing the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. The catalyst can be recovered unchanged at the end — its mass is the same before and after.

subsections.heading: The two named practicals
subsections.html:
Spec 3.15, 3.16 (practicals) · 2022 Q3 · 2023 Q7 · 2024 Q3 · 2025 Q1

1 — Marble chips + hydrochloric acid (surface area / concentration). CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). Flask on a balance, cotton wool plug, record mass every 20–30 s. Change one variable (chip size, or acid concentration), keep everything else the same: same mass of chips, same volume and temperature of acid.

2 — Catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (catalysts). Measure with a gas syringe; compare different solid catalysts by the initial gradient of the volume–time curve. Same volume and concentration of H₂O₂, same mass of catalyst, same temperature.

When the question says "explain how you would make it a fair test", name the actual variables kept constant — the generic phrase "fair test" scores nothing.

subsections.heading: Sketching the second curve
subsections.html:
2023 Q7b · 2024 Q3b

Asked almost every year: given the curve at one temperature (or concentration), draw the curve for a hotter / more concentrated / powdered version. Two marks, two rules:

  • Steeper at the start, beginning at exactly (0,0) — 2023: "the curve had to very obviously start at (0,0) — quite a lot missed the axes slightly."
  • Levels off at exactly the same final amount (same mass and moles of reactant → same product), just reached sooner. If the amount of reactant changed, only then does the plateau move.

The one template everything follows from

Rate questions are answered with frequency of successful collisions. Name the factor's effect on the particles, keep the word successful, and end with more collisions per unit time.

subsections.heading: Graph craft — where the easy marks go
subsections.html:
• Sharp pencil, plots exact to the nearest gridline, visible ×.
  • Best-fit curve: one single smooth line, no feathering, through the origin when the data starts there, level exactly at the plateau.
  • Reading a value or a tangent: show the construction lines on the graph — they carry marks on their own.
  • Second-condition sketch: steeper from (0,0), same plateau height.
  • Ignore an anomalous point when drawing the line — and if asked why an anomaly happened in a rates experiment, "forgot to stir" is the accepted cause on this school's papers.

questions.promptHtml: A student says: "Doubling the concentration doubles the energy of the collisions, so the reaction is faster." There is one correct claim and one wrong claim in that sentence. Which is which?
questions.answerHtml:
Correct: the reaction is faster.

Wrong: concentration does not change the energy of anything. The particles move at the same speed at the same temperature; there are simply more of them in the same volume, so collisions happen more frequently.

Energy language belongs only in temperature answers. The 2024 mark scheme capped concentration answers mentioning kinetic energy at 1 mark of 3 — this exact confusion.

questions.promptHtml: The same mass of marble is used in two runs — large chips, then the same mass ground to powder. Why does the powder react faster, and why is the final volume of CO₂ the same in both runs?
questions.answerHtml:
Faster: grinding exposes far more particles at the surface — greater surface area — so collisions between acid particles and carbonate particles happen more frequently.

Same final volume: the amount of CaCO₃ is unchanged — same mass, same moles — so the same moles of CO₂ are eventually made. Surface area changes how fast you get there, never how much you get.

On the graph: steeper start, same plateau. If your sketch's plateau moves, you have changed the amount, not the rate.

questions.promptHtml: Why does raising the temperature by only 10 °C roughly double the rate, when the collision frequency only rises by a few percent?
questions.answerHtml:
Because frequency is the small effect. The big effect is that the proportion of collisions with energy above the activation energy rises steeply with temperature — many collisions that used to bounce apart now react.

That is why the mark scheme insists on "more collisions have energy greater than the activation energy / a greater proportion are successful" as its own separate mark, and why merging it into "more collisions" loses it. Two different mechanisms: hitting harder (dominant) and hitting more often (minor).

questions.promptHtml: A catalyst does not appear in the chemical equation and its mass is unchanged at the end. So how can it possibly change the rate?
questions.answerHtml:
It takes part, then is regenerated. The catalyst offers the reaction an alternative pathway — a different route from reactants to products — whose activation energy is lower.

The particles' energies are unchanged, but the bar they must clear is lower, so a greater proportion of the same collisions are now successful.

Because the catalyst is chemically unchanged overall, a tiny amount works for a large amount of reactant, and it is still there — same mass — at the end. That "chemically unchanged at the end" phrase is the definition mark.

questions.promptHtml: Two identical H₂O₂ experiments run at 20 °C and 40 °C. Sketch both curves in your head: state three things the 40 °C curve does and one thing it must not do.
questions.answerHtml:
The 40 °C curve:

  1. starts at exactly (0,0), like the original;
  2. rises more steeply from the start;
  3. levels off sooner — but at the same final volume, because the amount of H₂O₂ is the same.

It must not level off at a higher or lower volume. Temperature changes the journey, not the destination — only changing the amount (or concentration and volume) of reactant moves the plateau.

questions.promptHtml: In the marble-chips experiment the reaction eventually stops while chips are still visible in the flask. What ran out, how would the balance tell you the reaction had stopped, and what would you see in the flask?
questions.answerHtml:
What ran out: the hydrochloric acid — the acid is the limiting reactant. "All the acid has reacted" is the accepted wording.

The balance: the mass stops decreasing — the reading stays constant. (On a graph: the curve levels off.)

In the flask: the fizzing/effervescence stops.

Note the logic: solid left over ⇒ the other reactant finished. This is the same limiting-reactant idea the calculations module uses — the excess is visible, the limiting reagent decides when it ends.

questions.promptHtml: Why is the rate of reaction greatest at the very start — and what is wrong with answering "because the particles have the most energy at the start"?
questions.answerHtml:
Right answer: at the start the concentration of the acid (the reactants in solution) is at its highest — the most particles per unit volume — so collisions are at their most frequent. As reactant is used up, collisions become rarer and the curve flattens.

The wrong answer: energy has nothing to do with it. The temperature is constant, so the particles' energies are the same at the start as at the end. The 2023 scheme explicitly rejected incorrect references to energy here.

questions.promptHtml: A student compares two catalysts for the decomposition of H₂O₂ by timing how long each run takes to collect 20 cm³ of oxygen. Name the three variables that must be kept the same, and explain which catalyst is better: the 40-second run or the 90-second run.
questions.answerHtml:
Keep the same: volume and concentration of hydrogen peroxide, mass of catalyst, and temperature. (Naming the actual variables is what scores — "make it fair" scores nothing.)

Better catalyst: the 40-second one. Less time to make the same volume of gas = faster rate. With time-based measurements the comparison flips: shorter time means faster, and rate ∝ 1/time.

subsections.html: Electrolysis is using electricity to force a compound apart. Everything on these papers reduces to three questions: can it conduct? — what arrives at each electrode? — what wins the discharge? Each has a fixed answer pattern.

subsections.heading: Why things conduct — and why solids never do
subsections.html:
Spec 1.55C, 1.56C · 2023 Q2b · 2024 Q6a

Conduction needs charged particles free to move. Three cases, and the papers test all three:

  • Metals conduct always: delocalised electrons move through the lattice.
  • Ionic compounds conduct only when molten or dissolved: the ions are freed to move. In the solid, the ions are locked in the lattice — the ions cannot move. Never say "the electrons can't move" for an ionic solid: 2024's scheme gave no marks if the answer was about electrons.
  • Covalent compounds do not conduct: no ions, no free electrons — no charged particles free to move.

The 2023 four-marker asked for magnesium and magnesium chloride in one answer, and the four marks were exactly: delocalised electrons · electrons can move · MgCl₂ only molten/in solution · ions free to move. Say which particle moves in which substance.

subsections.heading: The circuit: ions travel, electrodes swap electrons
subsections.html:
Spec 1.57C · 2024 Q6b

Cations (+) — metal ions and H⁺ — travel to the cathode (−), where they gain electrons (reduction). Anions (−) travel to the anode (+), where they lose electrons (oxidation).

2024's "explain how sodium forms" is the pattern answer: positive sodium ions are attracted to the negative electrode and each ion gains an electron (is reduced) to become an atom. Both halves, and the word ion throughout — the scheme rejected "sodium atoms/metal moves to the electrode".

OIL RIG — and saying it about the right species

Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain — and it is always the ion that does the gaining or losing. "The bromide ions lose electrons" scores; "bromine loses electrons" was explicitly rejected in 2025, and "magnesium gains electrons" in 2023.

subsections.heading: Half-equations — the four you write and the two rules that kill them
subsections.html:
Spec 1.59C · every paper

At the cathode (reduction — electrons on the left):

  • Metal deposits: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu · Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na (molten) · Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg
  • Hydrogen from solution: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂

At the anode (oxidation — electrons on the right):

  • Halogens: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ · 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻
  • Oxygen from solution: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ (equivalently 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻)

The two rules the commentary begs for: halogens are diatomic (Cl₂, never Cl or Cl₃ or Cl⁺), and the oxygen half-equation starts from water in a solution — 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ was the standard wrong answer in 2023 because a solution contains no O²⁻ ions. Balance atoms first, then make the charges balance with electrons.

subsections.heading: Which ion is discharged — reactivity decides
subsections.html:
Spec 1.58C · 2022 Q5b · 2024 Q6b(iv) · 2025 Q3b

A solution always contains the compound's ions plus H⁺ and OH⁻ from water. At each electrode only one species is discharged:

  • Cathode: the less reactive of the metal and hydrogen. Copper and silver (below hydrogen) deposit as metal; sodium, potassium, magnesium (above hydrogen) stay in solution and hydrogen bubbles off instead. That is why aqueous NaCl gives H₂, not sodium — "sodium is more reactive than hydrogen" is the one-mark answer.
  • Anode: a halide present → the halogen (Cl₂, Br₂). Otherwise (sulfate, nitrate) → oxygen from water.

The 2021 table question is this rule five times over: CuSO₄ → Cu + O₂ (H₂SO₄ left); K₂SO₄ → H₂ + O₂ (K₂SO₄ left — effectively electrolysing water); AgNO₃ → Ag + O₂ (HNO₃ left); KNO₃ → H₂ + O₂ (KNO₃ left).

subsections.heading: What you would see, and what's left behind
subsections.html:
2023 Q5 · 2025 Q3b

Observations are bubbles and colours, not chemical names: at the anode of CuSO₄ electrolysis you see "effervescence / bubbles" (the scheme ignored "oxygen"). Gas tests close the loop: lit splint → squeaky pop = hydrogen; glowing splint relights = oxygen; chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper. Lit and glowing are not interchangeable — 2024 rejected the glowing splint for hydrogen.

The solution changes too. Electrolysing NaCl(aq): H⁺ is removed at the cathode, leaving Na⁺ and OH⁻ — the solution near the cathode turns alkaline, universal indicator goes blue/purple, and the particle responsible is the hydroxide ion. In CuSO₄(aq) with inert electrodes the blue fades as Cu²⁺ is removed and the solution becomes sulfuric acid. And where do OH⁻ ions in a copper sulfate solution come from at all? From water (dissociating) — not "because the solution is alkaline"; it isn't.

subsections.heading: Redox beyond the electrodes
subsections.html:
Spec 2.20 · 2021 Q10b · 2024 Q5a · 2025 Q4b

Redox has two currencies, and the papers use both:

  • Oxygen: oxidation = gaining oxygen, reduction = losing it. Thermite: aluminium is oxidised (gains oxygen), iron(III) oxide is reduced (loses oxygen) — name the whole compound; 2024 penalised "iron is reduced". A reducing agent removes oxygen from something else (carbon in metal extraction); an oxidising agent gives it.
  • Electrons: the electrode definition — loss is oxidation, gain is reduction — and the reason every anode reaction "is an oxidation": the ions lose electrons.

A reaction is redox when both happen at once: in Mg + O₂, magnesium is oxidised and oxygen reduced. Say which species is oxidised and which is reduced — "oxidation and reduction happen at the same time" scored nothing in 2024.

The one sentence everything follows from

Ions move to the oppositely charged electrode; the ION gains or loses electrons there; reactivity decides which ion wins. If your answer names an atom or a metal where it means an ion, it is wrong.

questions.promptHtml: Solid sodium chloride sits between two connected electrodes and nothing happens. The moment it melts, a current flows and products appear. What changed — and why would the same experiment described with "electrons become free to move" score zero?
questions.answerHtml:
Melting frees the ions. In the solid, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are locked in a lattice by their attractions; they vibrate but cannot travel, so no charge can flow. Molten, the ions move: Na⁺ to the cathode, Cl⁻ to the anode — the moving ions are the current inside the electrolyte.

"Electrons become free" is a different (wrong) conduction story — that is how metals conduct. An ionic compound never conducts by electron flow; the charge carriers are ions, and the mark schemes reject electron answers outright.

questions.promptHtml: Electrolysing concentrated sodium chloride solution gives hydrogen at the cathode, yet molten sodium chloride gives sodium. Explain the difference — and what universal indicator near the cathode of the solution would show.
questions.answerHtml:
The solution contains a second cation: H⁺ from the water. At the cathode the less reactive species is discharged, and hydrogen is far less reactive than sodium — so H⁺ gains the electrons and H₂ bubbles off, while Na⁺ stays in solution. Molten NaCl has no water, no H⁺, no competition: sodium is the only choice.

Removing H⁺ leaves Na⁺ and OH⁻ behind — sodium hydroxide solution. Universal indicator near the cathode turns blue/purple, because hydroxide ions accumulate there. (2025's marker: most students never realised an alkali was forming, and few could name the OH⁻ ion as the reason.)

questions.promptHtml: Why must the oxygen half-equation in a solution start from water (2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻) when 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ balances perfectly well?
questions.answerHtml:
Balancing isn't the test — existing is. A half-equation must start from a species actually present, and a solution of copper sulfate or dilute acid contains Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻, H⁺, OH⁻ and H₂O — but no free O²⁻ ions. Oxide ions are only found inside solid or molten oxides.

The oxygen made at the anode really does come from water molecules (or equivalently the OH⁻ from water): 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, or 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ — both accepted, because both start from what is really there. This exact wrong answer, 2O²⁻, was the year group's favourite in 2023.

questions.promptHtml: "The magnesium gains two electrons at the cathode." The teacher's comment on this sentence used two exclamation marks. What exactly is wrong with it, and what does the correct sentence look like?
questions.answerHtml:
Before the electrons arrive there is no magnesium — there is a magnesium ion, Mg²⁺. The whole event at the cathode is the ion becoming magnesium: Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg. Saying "magnesium gains electrons" describes a neutral atom taking on electrons, which is not what happens and would make Mg²⁻.

Correct: "the magnesium ion gains two electrons (is reduced) to form a magnesium atom." The same precision is demanded at the anode: bromide ions lose electrons; chlorine doesn't lose anything — it is the product.

questions.promptHtml: In the water-electrolysis apparatus, twice the volume of gas collects over the cathode as over the anode — but the oxygen tube is always slightly under half. Explain both facts.
questions.answerHtml:
The 2 : 1 ratio: water is H₂O — the half-equations transfer four electrons to make 2H₂ for every O₂. Twice the moles of hydrogen means twice the volume, because equal moles of gas occupy equal volumes.

The shortfall: some of the oxygen dissolves in the water (oxygen is slightly soluble; the same reason less chlorine than hydrogen collects from NaCl(aq) — chlorine dissolves too). Not a leak, not an error — the accepted one-marker is "some oxygen dissolves".

Related staple: why add dilute acid to the water first? Pure water is a poor conductor; the acid increases its conductivity. (Not "helps carry the current" — name the property.)

questions.promptHtml: The thermite reaction is 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe. The 2024 marker complained that "many just said oxidation and reduction are occurring at the same time" and that "many said IRON was reduced rather than IRON OXIDE". Write the answer that scores both marks.
questions.answerHtml:
"Aluminium is oxidised because it gains oxygen (→ Al₂O₃), and iron(III) oxide is reduced because it loses oxygen (→ Fe)."

Two named species, two named directions, each tied to oxygen. The two rejected shapes: (1) restating the definition of redox without naming anything; (2) "iron is reduced" — iron is the product; the thing that lost oxygen is the oxide. The electron version also scores: iron(III) ions gain electrons.

Bonus connection: aluminium here is the reducing agent — it removes the oxygen — exactly the role carbon plays in extracting iron in the metal-extraction module.

questions.promptHtml: Copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert graphite electrodes. Predict what happens at each electrode, what you would see, and what the solution contains at the end.
questions.answerHtml:
Cathode: copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu — a pink/brown coating of copper grows on the electrode.

Anode: no halide present, so oxygen from water: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ — you see effervescence/bubbles (that is the observation; "oxygen" is a name, not a sight).

End state: Cu²⁺ is progressively removed, so the blue colour fades; H⁺ accumulates with the SO₄²⁻, leaving dilute sulfuric acid. This is 2021's products-table row and 2023 Q5 in one story.
